## 1. Start with the essential workflow

### When a technician creates a repair
**Trigger:** New repair form submitted.

**The form asks:**
- Customer name
- Phone number
- Device model
- Problem
- Technician
- Parts used
- Estimated price
- Deposit/payment status

**Automatic actions:**
1. Create a job ID, e.g. `REP-2025-001`.
2. Set status to `Received`.
3. Save repair in the Repairs table.
4. Send customer message:

> “Hi {Name}, we received your {Device Model}. Your repair reference is {Job ID}. We will update you when it is ready.”

5. Notify the assigned technician.

---

## 2. Automatically reduce inventory

Do **not** reduce stock just because someone opens a repair ticket. The part may not actually be used.

**Best trigger:** Technician changes repair status to `In Repair` or `Completed` and confirms the part(s) used.

Example:

| Repair ID | Part Used | Quantity Used |
|---|---|---:|
| REP-001 | iPhone 11 Screen | 1 |
| REP-001 | iPhone 11 Battery | 1 |

**Automation:**
- Find the matching part in the Inventory table.
- Subtract `Quantity Used` from current stock.
- Add a record to a Stock Movements table.
- Check whether remaining stock is below reorder level.

Example:

| Part | Before | Used | After |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| iPhone 11 Screen | 4 | 1 | 3 |

This is much safer than simply subtracting one part from a dropdown, especially when one repair needs multiple parts.

---

## 3. Low-stock alert automation

In your **Inventory** table, add these fields:

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Part Name | iPhone 11 Screen |
| Current Quantity | 3 |
| Reorder Level | 3 |
| Supplier | PhoneParts Portugal |
| Supplier Contact | email / WhatsApp |
| Needs Restock | Yes/No |

### Formula logic
`Needs Restock = Current Quantity <= Reorder Level`

**Trigger:** Needs Restock changes to “Yes.”

**Actions:**
1. Send an email or WhatsApp to the owner.
2. Create a “Purchase Order Needed” record.
3. Optionally prepare a supplier message.

Example owner alert:

> ⚠️ Low stock: iPhone 11 Screen  
> Remaining: 3  
> Reorder level: 3  
> Supplier: PhoneParts Portugal

Example supplier draft:

> Hello, we need to order 10 × iPhone 11 screens. Please confirm availability and delivery time.

Keep supplier ordering as **approval required** at first. The system suggests it; the owner taps “Approve Order.”

---

## 4. Automatic customer repair updates

Create repair statuses:

- Received
- Diagnosing
- Waiting for customer approval
- Waiting for parts
- In repair
- Ready for pickup
- Completed
- Cancelled

### Automation rules

| Trigger | Automatic message |
|---|---|
| Status = Received | “We received your device.” |
| Status = Waiting for customer approval | “The estimate is €{Price}. Reply YES to approve.” |
| Status = Waiting for parts | “We are waiting for a replacement part. Expected update: {Date}.” |
| Status = Ready for pickup | “Your device is ready for collection.” |
| Status = Completed | “Thanks for choosing us. Please leave a review.” |

Example ready-for-pickup message:

> Hi {Customer Name}, your {Device Model} is ready for pickup.  
> Total: €{Final Price}.  
> Repair reference: {Job ID}.  
> Please bring your receipt when collecting it.

Use WhatsApp Business, SMS, or email. For Portugal, WhatsApp will usually get the best response.

---

## 5. Automatic follow-up and review request

**Trigger:** Repair is marked `Completed`.

**Actions:**
- After 2–3 days: send follow-up.
- After 7 days: request a Google review.
- After 90 days: warranty-expiry reminder, if the shop offers warranty.

### Follow-up message
> Hi {Name}, just checking that your {Device Model} is working well after the repair. Reply here if you need any help.

### Review request
> Thanks again for choosing {Shop Name}. If you were happy with the repair, a short Google review would really help our local business: {Google Review Link}

Do not send this to customers with an unresolved complaint or a cancelled repair.

---

## 6. Predictive restock automation

After the shop has used the app for a month or two, add this.

For each part, calculate:

- How many units were used in the last 30 days
- Average daily usage
- Days until stock runs out
- Recommended reorder quantity

Example:

| Part | Stock | Used Last 30 Days | Avg/day | Estimated Days Left |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| iPhone 11 Screen | 6 | 15 | 0.5 | 12 days |

**Alert rule:**
If estimated days left is below 14 days, notify owner:

> Forecast: iPhone 11 Screens may run out in 12 days based on recent repairs. Recommended order: 10 units.

This is a useful “AI” feature, but it is really simple inventory forecasting—and very valuable.

---

## 7. Best simple tech stack

For a first real customer, use:

- **Glide**

The most important point is:

## Only reduce stock when the technician confirms the part was actually used

This prevents the biggest inventory problem: the app showing stock that is wrong.

A repair may be opened for an iPhone 11 screen replacement, but then:

- the customer does not approve the quote;
- the device has extra damage;
- the technician finds the screen was not the issue;
- the customer takes the phone back;
- the part is ordered but not installed yet.

If stock drops immediately when the repair ticket is created, the shop’s inventory becomes inaccurate.

---

# Correct process

Use three separate stages:

1. **Repair created**  
   The shop records what the customer says is wrong.  
   No inventory changes yet.

2. **Part reserved or planned** *(optional)*  
   The technician may select likely parts needed.  
   Still do not subtract from real stock—unless you build a proper reservation system.

3. **Part actually installed**  
   Technician confirms the part and quantity used.  
   Now the app automatically subtracts it from inventory.

The rule is simple:

> A job request is not stock usage.  
> A confirmed installed part is stock usage.

---

# The tables you need

A reliable version should have at least four tables.

## 1. Inventory table

This is the live count of every physical part in the shop.

| Part ID | Part Name | Compatible Models | Quantity in Stock | Reorder Level | Cost Price | Selling Price |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| P-001 | iPhone 11 Screen OLED | iPhone 11 | 6 | 3 | €32 | €89 |
| P-002 | iPhone 11 Battery | iPhone 11 | 8 | 3 | €18 | €55 |
| P-003 | Samsung A52 Screen | Samsung A52 | 2 | 2 | €29 | €79 |

The important fields are:

- **Quantity in Stock** — how many physical items are available now.
- **Reorder Level** — the minimum safe amount.
- **Cost Price** — useful for profit calculations.
- **Supplier** — useful for reordering later.

---

## 2. Repairs table

This is one row per customer repair.

| Job ID | Customer | Device | Issue | Technician | Status | Estimated Price | Final Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---:|---:|
| REP-001 | João Silva | iPhone 11 | Cracked screen | Miguel | In Repair | €89 | — |
| REP-002 | Ana Costa | Samsung A52 | Battery drains fast | Pedro | Received | €55 | — |

Do not put only one “Part Used” field directly in this table if you can avoid it.

Why? One repair can use multiple parts:

- screen;
- battery;
- charging connector;
- adhesive;
- camera glass;
- screws or small components.

Instead, use a separate table for the parts used in each repair.

---

## 3. Repair Parts Used table

This is the most important table for automation.

Each row represents one part used for one repair.

| Usage ID | Job ID | Part ID | Part Name | Quantity Used | Confirmed By | Date | Stock Deducted? |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---|---|---|
| USE-001 | REP-001 | P-001 | iPhone 11 Screen OLED | 1 | Miguel | 2025-03-08 | Yes |
| USE-002 | REP-001 | P-010 | Screen adhesive | 1 | Miguel | 2025-03-08 | Yes |

This lets the technician select several parts for one repair.

Most importantly, the **Stock Deducted?** field prevents the same item from being deducted twice.

---

## 4. Stock Movements table

This gives the shop an audit trail: every stock change has a reason.

| Movement ID | Date | Part ID | Type | Quantity Change | Reason | Job ID | Staff |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---|---|---|
| MOV-001 | 2025-03-08 | P-001 | Used in repair | -1 | Screen replacement | REP-001 | Miguel |
| MOV-002 | 2025-03-07 | P-001 | Delivery received | +10 | Supplier delivery | — | Owner |
| MOV-003 | 2025-03-08 | P-001 | Adjustment | -1 | Damaged part | — | Owner |

This table is extremely useful when the owner says:

> “The app says we should have six screens, but I can only see five.”

They can check every movement and find the reason.

---

Here is the clean workflow your app should follow.

## Step 1: Technician opens or updates a repair

Example:

- Job ID: `REP-001`
- Device: iPhone 11
- Status: `In Repair`

The technician sees a button:

> **Add part used**

They select:

- Part: iPhone 11 Screen OLED
- Quantity: 1
- Confirm installation: Yes

At this stage, the app creates a row in **Repair Parts Used**.

---

## Step 2: The app validates the stock

Before deducting anything, the automation checks:

> Is quantity in stock greater than or equal to quantity requested?

For example:

- Stock: 6 screens
- Technician needs: 1 screen
- Result: allowed

If there are zero screens left, the app should block or warn the technician:

> Not enough stock available.  
> Current stock: 0  
> Needed:

Another important aspect is the **low-stock and reorder system**. An inventory app is only valuable if it helps the shop avoid losing repair jobs because a common screen, battery, or charging port is unavailable.

## The goal

The owner should not need to remember:

- which parts are running low;
- which models are repaired most often;
- when to order;
- which supplier to contact;
- how many units to buy.

The app should monitor this automatically and show only clear actions:

> “Order iPhone 11 screens.”  
> “Samsung A52 batteries are nearly out.”  
> “You have enough iPhone XR screens for about 9 days.”

---

# Use two stock levels, not one

For every inventory item, store:

| Field | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---:|
| Current stock | Parts physically available now | 4 |
| Reorder level | Point at which the owner should order more | 3 |
| Target stock | Ideal quantity after ordering | 10 |
| Supplier lead time | Days supplier normally takes to deliver | 2 days |
| Average weekly usage | Parts used each week | 5 |

The key difference:

- **Reorder level** means: “Order now.”
- **Target stock** means: “Order enough to get back to this level.”

Example:

- Current stock: 2 iPhone 11 screens
- Reorder level: 3
- Target stock: 10

The app recommends ordering:

`10 − 2 = 8 screens`

That is much better than merely sending “low stock.”

---

# Basic low-stock automation

Start with this simple rule:

```text
If Current Stock <= Reorder Level
then Needs Restock = Yes
```

Example inventory:

| Part | Current Stock | Reorder Level | Result |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| iPhone 11 Screen | 2 | 3 | Order now |
| iPhone 11 Battery | 6 | 3 | No action |
| Samsung A52 Screen | 1 | 2 | Order now |

When the stock update occurs—because a technician used a part—the automation checks that rule immediately.

## Trigger

> A stock movement is recorded, or Current Stock changes.

## Actions

1. Check whether the part is at/below reorder level.
2. Mark the part as `Needs Restock`.
3. Create a reorder task or purchase-order draft.
4. Send one message to the owner.
5. Avoid sending the same alert repeatedly.

---

# Avoid notification spam

A bad system sends the owner the same alert every time a repair is updated.

Instead, add these fields:

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Needs Restock | Yes / No |
| Low Stock Alert Sent | Yes / No |
| Last Alert Date | Date/time |
| Reorder Status | Not needed / Draft / Ordered / Received |

### Correct alert rule

Send an alert only when:

```text
Needs Restock = Yes
AND Low Stock Alert Sent = No
```

After sending the alert:

```text
Low Stock Alert Sent = Yes
Last Alert Date = now
Reorder Status = Draft
```

When new stock arrives and the quantity goes back above the reorder level, reset:

```text
Needs Restock = No
Low Stock Alert Sent = No
```

Now the next genuine low-stock event can create a fresh alert.

---

# Create a purchase-order draft automatically

Instead of only notifying the owner, create a **Purchase Orders** table.

| Order ID | Supplier | Part | Qty Recommended | Status | Date Created |
|---|---|---|---:|---|---|
| PO-001 | PhoneParts Portugal | iPhone 11 Screen | 8 | Draft | 2025-03-08 |
| PO-002 | GSM Parts Supplier | Samsung A52 Screen | 9 | Draft | 2025-03-08 |

Recommended quantity formula:

```text
Target Stock − Current Stock
```

Example:

- Target stock = 10
- Current stock = 2
- Recommended quantity = 8

The owner sees a screen called **Parts to Order**, checks the suggested quantities, and taps:

> Approve order

At first, do not automatically place supplier orders. Supplier stock, prices, and delivery terms may change. Human approval prevents costly mistakes.

---

# Supplier information

In the Inventory table, keep supplier details per part.

| Part | Preferred Supplier | Supplier Phone | Supplier Email | Supplier Part Code |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone 11 Screen OLED | PhoneParts Portugal | +351... | orders@... | IP11-OLED-BLK |
| Samsung A52 Battery | GSM Wholesale | +351... | sales@... | SA52-BAT-01 |

When the owner approves an order, the app can generate a ready-made WhatsApp or email message:

> Hello, I would like to order:  
> - 8 × iPhone 11 OLED Screens, part code IP11-OLED-BLK  
> - 5 × iPhone 11 Batteries, part code IP11-BAT-02  
>   
> Please confirm availability, total price, and delivery time.  
> Thank you, {Shop Name}.

This saves time without pretending the order was placed automatically.

---

# Receiving stock correctly

When a supplier delivery arrives, the owner should not manually overwrite the stock number.

They should use a form:

> **Receive stock delivery**

Fields:

- Supplier
- Part
- Quantity received
- Unit cost
- Invoice number
- Delivery date
- Notes, such as damaged/missing items

Example:

| Part | Current Stock Before | Delivery | New Stock |
|---|---:|---:|---:|

A few important things are easy to overlook when building this for a real repair shop.

## 1. “Stock in the app” is not automatically real stock

The app is only accurate if staff actually record:

- parts installed;
- new deliveries received;
- damaged parts;
- returns to supplier;
- parts taken for another purpose;
- stock corrections after physical counting.

If technicians install parts but forget to press **Add Part Used**, the system becomes wrong.

### Practical solution
Make the workflow unavoidable:

> A repair cannot be marked **Completed** until the technician confirms either:
> - parts used were logged, or
> - “No part used” was selected.

Add a required field:

```text
Parts confirmation:
[ ] Parts logged
[ ] No part used
```

This is more important than adding AI.

---

## 2. A repair can use more than one part

A cracked-screen repair may use:

- screen;
- adhesive;
- frame;
- camera lens;
- screws;
- waterproof seal.

If your app has only one “Part Used” field, it will fail quickly.

### Practical solution
Use the `PartsUsed` table with one row per item.

For one repair:

| Job ID | Part | Quantity |
|---|---|---:|
| REP-001 | iPhone 11 OLED Screen | 1 |
| REP-001 | Screen Adhesive | 1 |
| REP-001 | Camera Lens Glass | 1 |

This also makes profit tracking possible later.

---

## 3. Reserved stock and installed stock are different

A technician may decide that an iPhone 12 screen will probably be needed. That does not mean it has been installed.

If you subtract the screen too early, the app may show there is no stock even though it is still on the shelf.

### Better approach

Use three quantities:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Physical Stock | Actual items in the shop |
| Reserved Stock | Items set aside for approved repairs |
| Available Stock | Physical Stock − Reserved Stock |

For the first version, you can skip reservations entirely and only deduct on installation.

Later, add a **Reserve Part** button for expensive or rare parts.

---

## 4. Parts have variations that look similar but are not interchangeable

“iPhone 11 screen” may not be enough detail. The shop may stock:

- LCD;
- OLED;
- soft OLED;
- refurbished original;
- black or white;
- with/without frame;
- different suppliers and quality grades.

If staff choose the wrong item, both stock and profit data become wrong.

### Practical solution
Give every part a clear internal name and code:

```text
IPH11-OLED-SOFT-BLK
IPH11-LCD-BLK
IPH11-BAT-STD
SAM-A52-SCR-AMOLED
```

In the app, show a friendly name:

> iPhone 11 — Soft OLED Screen — Black

Do not use vague dropdown options such as only “iPhone Screen.”

---

## 5. Do not automatically message customers without consent

Automated WhatsApp, SMS, and marketing messages can create privacy and compliance issues.

Separate:

- **service messages** — repair received, estimate ready, phone ready;
- **marketing messages** — review requests, discounts, promotions, reminders.

A customer may reasonably expect service updates. Marketing messages should be optional.

### Practical solution
In the Repairs table, add:

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Service Updates Allowed | Yes |
| Marketing Consent | No |
| Preferred Contact Method | WhatsApp |

Only send review requests or offers when `Marketing Consent = Yes`.

Also, do not place sensitive details in messages. Say:

> “Your device is ready for collection.”

Do not say:

> “Your iPhone was repaired because the private photos recovery failed…”

---

## 6. The app needs a way to handle mistakes

Someone will eventually:

- select the wrong part;
- type quantity `10` instead of `1`;
- mark a repair completed too early;
- receive stock twice;
- lose or damage a part.

If people can directly edit the stock number, you will lose the audit trail.

### Practical solution
Use **adjustment records**, not direct edits.

Create a stock adjustment form:

```text
Part: iPhone 11 Screen OLED
Adjustment: -1
Reason: Damaged during installation
Staff member: Miguel
Notes: Display arrived defective
```

The app creates a movement:

| Type | Quantity Change |
|---|---:|
| Damage / Adjustment | -1 |

The owner can later see exactly why stock changed.

---

## 7. Returns, warranties, and failed repairs need their own flow

A customer may return after a screen replacement because the replacement part failed under warranty.

If the shop installs another screen, the app should record:

- a new part used;
- the warranty repair reference;
- whether the defective part was returned to the supplier;
- whether supplier credit is expected.

### Add fields to Repairs

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Warranty Repair? | Yes |
| Original Job ID | REP-001 |
| Supplier Return Needed? | Yes |
| Warranty Expiry Date | 2025-06-08 |

This matters because warranty work can otherwise look like “free labour with missing stock.”

---

## 8. You need a physical stock-count routine

Even excellent software cannot replace counting the shelf.

Start simple:

- Count high-value and fast-moving parts weekly.
- Count everything monthly.
- Compare physical count against app count.
- Create an adjustment movement if there is a difference.

Example:

| Part | App Count | Physical Count | Difference | Action |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| iPhone 11 OLED Screen | 6

Yes — for the inventory/repair app, make the repetitive work automatic with a simple trigger → action setup.

## 1. Start with the essential workflow

### When a technician creates a repair
**Trigger:** New repair form submitted.

**The form asks:**
- Customer name
- Phone number
- Device model
- Problem
- Technician
- Parts used
- Estimated price
- Deposit/payment status

**Automatic actions:**
1. Create a job ID, e.g. `REP-2025-001`.
2. Set status to `Received`.
3. Save repair in the Repairs table.
4. Send customer message:

> “Hi {Name}, we received your {Device Model}. Your repair reference is {Job ID}. We will update you when it is ready.”

5. Notify the assigned technician.

---

## 2. Automatically reduce inventory

Do **not** reduce stock just because someone opens a repair ticket. The part may not actually be used.

**Best trigger:** Technician changes repair status to `In Repair` or `Completed` and confirms the part(s) used.

Example:

| Repair ID | Part Used | Quantity Used |
|---|---|---:|
| REP-001 | iPhone 11 Screen | 1 |
| REP-001 | iPhone 11 Battery | 1 |

**Automation:**
- Find the matching part in the Inventory table.
- Subtract `Quantity Used` from current stock.
- Add a record to a Stock Movements table.
- Check whether remaining stock is below reorder level.

Example:

| Part | Before | Used | After |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| iPhone 11 Screen | 4 | 1 | 3 |

This is much safer than simply subtracting one part from a dropdown, especially when one repair needs multiple parts.

---

## 3. Low-stock alert automation

In your **Inventory** table, add these fields:

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Part Name | iPhone 11 Screen |
| Current Quantity | 3 |
| Reorder Level | 3 |
| Supplier | PhoneParts Portugal |
| Supplier Contact | email / WhatsApp |
| Needs Restock | Yes/No |

### Formula logic
`Needs Restock = Current Quantity <= Reorder Level`

**Trigger:** Needs Restock changes to “Yes.”

**Actions:**
1. Send an email or WhatsApp to the owner.
2. Create a “Purchase Order Needed” record.
3. Optionally prepare a supplier message.

Example owner alert:

> ⚠️ Low stock: iPhone 11 Screen  
> Remaining: 3  
> Reorder level: 3  
> Supplier: PhoneParts Portugal

Example supplier draft:

> Hello, we need to order 10 × iPhone 11 screens. Please confirm availability and delivery time.

Keep supplier ordering as **approval required** at first. The system suggests it; the owner taps “Approve Order.”

---

## 4. Automatic customer repair updates

Create repair statuses:

- Received
- Diagnosing
- Waiting for customer approval
- Waiting for parts
- In repair
- Ready for pickup
- Completed
- Cancelled

### Automation rules

| Trigger | Automatic message |
|---|---|
| Status = Received | “We received your device.” |
| Status = Waiting for customer approval | “The estimate is €{Price}. Reply YES to approve.” |
| Status = Waiting for parts | “We are waiting for a replacement part. Expected update: {Date}.” |
| Status = Ready for pickup | “Your device is ready for collection.” |
| Status = Completed | “Thanks for choosing us. Please leave a review.” |

Example ready-for-pickup message:

> Hi {Customer Name}, your {Device Model} is ready for pickup.  
> Total: €{Final Price}.  
> Repair reference: {Job ID}.  
> Please bring your receipt when collecting it.

Use WhatsApp Business, SMS, or email. For Portugal, WhatsApp will usually get the best response.

---

## 5. Automatic follow-up and review request

**Trigger:** Repair is marked `Completed`.

**Actions:**
- After 2–3 days: send follow-up.
- After 7 days: request a Google review.
- After 90 days: warranty-expiry reminder, if the shop offers warranty.

### Follow-up message
> Hi {Name}, just checking that your {Device Model} is working well after the repair. Reply here if you need any help.

### Review request
> Thanks again for choosing {Shop Name}. If you were happy with the repair, a short Google review would really help our local business: {Google Review Link}

Do not send this to customers with an unresolved complaint or a cancelled repair.

---

## 6. Predictive restock automation

After the shop has used the app for a month or two, add this.

For each part, calculate:

- How many units were used in the last 30 days
- Average daily usage
- Days until stock runs out

# Correct process

Use three separate stages:

1. **Repair created**  
   The shop records what the customer says is wrong.  
   No inventory changes yet.

2. **Part reserved or planned** *(optional)*  
   The technician may select likely parts needed.  
   Still do not subtract from real stock—unless you build a proper reservation system.

3. **Part actually installed**  
   Technician confirms the part and quantity used.  
   Now the app automatically subtracts it from inventory.

The rule is simple:

> A job request is not stock usage.  
> A confirmed installed part is stock usage.

# Use two stock levels, not one

For every inventory item, store:

| Field | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---:|
| Current stock | Parts physically available now | 4 |
| Reorder level | Point at which the owner should order more | 3 |
| Target stock | Ideal quantity after ordering | 10 |
| Supplier lead time | Days supplier normally takes to deliver | 2 days |
| Average weekly usage | Parts used each week | 5 |

The key difference:

- **Reorder level** means: “Order now.”
- **Target stock** means: “Order enough to get back to this level.”

Example:

- Current stock: 2 iPhone 11 screens
- Reorder level: 3
- Target stock: 10

The app recommends ordering:

`10 − 2 = 8 screens`

That is much better than merely sending “low stock.”

# Basic low-stock automation

Start with this simple rule:

```text
If Current Stock <= Reorder Level
then Needs Restock = Yes
```

Example inventory:

| Part | Current Stock | Reorder Level | Result |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| iPhone 11 Screen | 2 | 3 | Order now |
| iPhone 11 Battery | 6 | 3 | No action |
| Samsung A52 Screen | 1 | 2 | Order now |

When the stock update occurs—because a technician used a part—the automation checks that rule immediately.

## Trigger

> A stock movement is recorded, or Current Stock changes.

## Actions

1. Check whether the part is at/below reorder level.
2. Mark the part as `Needs Restock`.
3. Create a reorder task or purchase-order draft.
4. Send one message to the owner.
5. Avoid sending the same alert repeatedly.

# Avoid notification spam

A bad system sends the owner the same alert every time a repair is updated.

Instead, add these fields:

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Needs Restock | Yes / No |
| Low Stock Alert Sent | Yes / No |
| Last Alert Date | Date/time |
| Reorder Status | Not needed / Draft / Ordered / Received |

### Correct alert rule

Send an alert only when:

```text
Needs Restock = Yes
AND Low Stock Alert Sent = No
```

After sending the alert:

```text
Low Stock Alert Sent = Yes
Last Alert Date = now
Reorder Status = Draft
```

When new stock arrives and the quantity goes back above the reorder level, reset:

```text
Needs Restock = No
Low Stock Alert Sent = No
```

Now the next genuine low-stock event can create a fresh alert.

A few important things are easy to overlook when building this for a real repair shop.

## 1. “Stock in the app” is not automatically real stock

The app is only accurate if staff actually record:

- parts installed;
- new deliveries received;
- damaged parts;
- returns to supplier;
- parts taken for another purpose;
- stock corrections after physical counting.

If technicians install parts but forget to press **Add Part Used**, the system becomes wrong.

### Practical solution
Make the workflow unavoidable:

> A repair cannot be marked **Completed** until the technician confirms either:
> - parts used were logged, or
> - “No part used” was selected.

Add a required field:

```text
Parts confirmation:
[ ] Parts logged
[ ] No part used
```

This is more important than adding AI.

---

## 2. A repair can use more than one part

A cracked-screen repair may use:

- screen;
- adhesive;
- frame;
- camera lens;
- screws;
- waterproof seal.

If your app has only one “Part Used” field, it will fail quickly.

### Practical solution
Use the `PartsUsed` table with one row per item.

For one repair:

| Job ID | Part | Quantity |
|---|---|---:|
| REP-001 | iPhone 11 OLED Screen | 1 |
| REP-001 | Screen Adhesive | 1 |
| REP-001 | Camera Lens Glass | 1 |

This also makes profit tracking possible later.

---

## 3. Reserved stock and installed stock are different

A technician may decide that an iPhone 12 screen will probably be needed. That does not mean it has been installed.

If you subtract the screen too early, the app may show there is no stock even though it is still on the shelf.

### Better approach

Use three quantities:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Physical Stock | Actual items in the shop |
| Reserved Stock | Items set aside for approved repairs |
| Available Stock | Physical Stock − Reserved Stock |

For the first version, you can skip reservations entirely and only deduct on installation.

Later, add a **Reserve Part** button for expensive or rare parts.

---

## 4. Parts have variations that look similar but are not interchangeable

“iPhone 11 screen” may not be enough detail. The shop may stock:

- LCD;
- OLED;
- soft OLED;
- refurbished original;
- black or white;
- with/without frame;
- different suppliers and quality grades.

If staff choose the wrong item, both stock and profit data become wrong.

### Practical solution
Give every part a clear internal name and code:

```text
IPH11-OLED-SOFT-BLK
IPH11-LCD-BLK
IPH11-BAT-STD
SAM-A52-SCR-AMOLED
```

In the app, show a friendly name:

> iPhone 11 — Soft OLED Screen — Black

Do not use vague dropdown options such as only “iPhone Screen.”

---

## 5. Do not automatically message customers without consent

Automated WhatsApp, SMS, and marketing messages can create privacy and compliance issues.

Separate:

- **service messages** — repair received, estimate ready, phone ready;
- **marketing messages** — review requests, discounts, promotions, reminders.

A customer may reasonably expect service updates. Marketing messages should be optional.

### Practical solution
In the Repairs table, add:

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Service Updates Allowed | Yes |
| Marketing Consent | No |
| Preferred Contact Method | WhatsApp |

Only send review requests or offers when `Marketing Consent = Yes`.

Also, do not place sensitive details in messages. Say:

> “Your device is ready for collection.”

Do not say:

> “Your iPhone was repaired because the private photos recovery failed…”

---

## 6. The app needs a way to handle mistakes

Someone will eventually:

- select the wrong part;
- type quantity `10` instead of `1`;
- mark a repair completed too early;
- receive stock twice;
- lose or damage a part.

If people can directly edit the stock number, you will lose the audit trail.

### Practical solution
Use **adjustment records**, not direct edits.

Create a stock adjustment form:

```text
Part: iPhone 11 Screen OLED
Adjustment: -1
Reason: Damaged during installation
Staff member: Miguel
Notes: Display arrived defective
```

The app creates a movement:

| Type | Quantity Change |
|---|---:|
| Damage / Adjustment | -1 |

The owner can later see exactly why stock changed.
